title: Falling Objects
lead: Falling objects form an interesting class of motion problems, and the most remarkable fact about them is that, when air resistance is negligible, all objects at a given location fall with the same constant acceleration, whatever their mass. This section names that acceleration, the acceleration due to gravity $\kg$, applies the kinematic equations for constant acceleration to objects thrown up, thrown down or simply dropped, and shows how the distance and the time of a fall give the local value of $\kg$.
objectives: Describe the effects of gravity on objects in motion.
Describe the motion of objects that are in free fall.
Calculate the position and velocity of objects in free fall.
summary_html:
• An object in free-fall experiences constant acceleration if air resistance is negligible.
  • On Earth, all free-falling objects have an acceleration due to gravity $\kg$, which averages $$\kg = 9.80\ \text{m/s}^2.$$
  • Whether the acceleration $\ka$ should be taken as $+\kg$ or $-\kg$ is determined by your choice of coordinate system. If you choose the upward direction as positive, $\ka = -\kg = -9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$ is negative. In the opposite case, $\ka = +\kg = 9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$ is positive. Since acceleration is constant, the kinematic equations above can be applied with the appropriate $+\kg$ or $-\kg$ substituted for $\ka$.
  • For objects in free-fall, up is normally taken as positive for displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
notes: Problems 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18 have no answer in the book’s key and are left out, the PhET Equation Grapher note is left out, and the three strategy sketches (Figures 2.38, 2.40 and 2.43) are kept as originals of the demos that follow their examples rather than as figures of their own.
exercises_lead: Assume air resistance is negligible unless otherwise stated.

figures.original_caption: A hammer and a feather will fall with the same constant acceleration if air resistance is considered negligible. This is a general characteristic of gravity not unique to Earth, as astronaut David R. Scott demonstrated on the Moon in 1971, where the acceleration due to gravity is only 1.67 m/s².

Vertical position, vertical velocity, and vertical acceleration vs. time for a rock thrown vertically up at the edge of a cliff. Notice that velocity changes linearly with time and that acceleration is constant. Misconception Alert! Notice that the position vs. time graph shows vertical position only. It is easy to get the impression that the graph shows some horizontal motion—the shape of the graph looks like the path of a projectile. But this is not the case; the horizontal axis is time, not space. The actual path of the rock in space is straight up, and straight down.

(a) A person throws a rock straight up, as explored in Example 2.14. The arrows are velocity vectors at 0, 1.00, 2.00, and 3.00 s. (b) A person throws a rock straight down from a cliff with the same initial speed as before, as in Example 2.15. Note that at the same distance below the point of release, the rock has the same velocity in both cases.

Positions and velocities of a metal ball released from rest when air resistance is negligible. Velocity is seen to increase linearly with time while displacement increases with time squared. Acceleration is a constant and is equal to gravitational acceleration.

exercises.prompt: A chunk of ice breaks off a glacier and falls 30.0 meters before it hits the water. Assuming it falls freely (there is no air resistance), how long does it take to hit the water?

answer.hint: The ice starts from rest, so the position equation has only the $\kt^2$ term on the right; take $\ky = -30.0$ m and $\ka = -\kg$.
answer.solution: We know that initial position $\kyo = 0$, final position $\ky = -30.0\ \text{m}$, and $\ka = -\kg = -9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$. We can then use the equation $\ky = \kyo + \kvo\kt + \tfrac{1}{2}\ka\kt^2$ to solve for $\kt$. Inserting $\ka = -\kg$, we obtain $$\begin{aligned}\ky &= 0 + 0 - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2\\ \kt^2 &= \frac{2\ky}{-\kg}\\ \kt &= \pm\sqrt{\frac{2\ky}{-\kg}} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{2(-30.0\ \text{m})}{-9.80\ \text{m/s}^2}} = \pm\sqrt{6.12\ \text{s}^2} = 2.47\ \text{s} \approx 2.5\ \text{s}\end{aligned}$$ where we take the positive value as the physically relevant answer. Thus, it takes about 2.5 seconds for the piece of ice to hit the water.

exercises.prompt: Observing a spacecraft land on a distant asteroid, scientists notice that the craft is falling at a rate of 5 m/s. When it is 100 m closer to the surface of the asteroid, the craft reports a velocity of 8 m/s. According to their data, what is the approximate gravitational acceleration on this asteroid?

answer.hint: Two velocities and the distance between them, with no time given, call for $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 + 2\ka(\ky - \kyo)$, solved for $\ka$.

exercises.prompt: What is the acceleration of a rock thrown straight upward on the way up? At the top of its flight? On the way down?

answer.solution: The acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity at every point of the flight: $-9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$ with up taken as positive, on the way up, at the top, and on the way down. Only the velocity changes. As the discussion of Example 2.14 notes, at the highest point the velocity is zero, but the acceleration is still $-9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$, and it is the same for the whole trip, while the rock is moving up and while it is moving down.

exercises.prompt: An object that is thrown straight up falls back to Earth. This is one-dimensional motion. (a) When is its velocity zero? (b) Does its velocity change direction? (c) Does the acceleration due to gravity have the same sign on the way up as on the way down?

answer.solution: (a) The velocity is zero for an instant at the highest point, when the object has stopped rising and has not yet begun to fall. (b) Yes. The velocity is positive, upward, on the way up and negative, downward, on the way down, so it changes direction at the highest point. (c) Yes. The acceleration due to gravity points downward the whole time, so with up taken as positive it is $-\kg$ on the way up, at the top, and on the way down; its sign never changes.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you throw a rock nearly straight up at a coconut in a palm tree, and the rock misses on the way up but hits the coconut on the way down. Neglecting air resistance, how does the speed of the rock when it hits the coconut on the way down compare with what it would have been if it had hit the coconut on the way up? Is it more likely to dislodge the coconut on the way up or down? Explain.

answer.solution: Because only the acceleration due to gravity acts on the rock, its speed depends only on its initial speed and its height, as Example 2.15 shows. At the height of the coconut the rock therefore has the same speed on the way down as it had on the way up; only the direction of its velocity is reversed. Since the speed of the blow is the same either way, the rock is no more likely to dislodge the coconut on the way down than on the way up on the basis of speed; what differs is only that on the way down the rock strikes the coconut from above.

exercises.prompt: If an object is thrown straight up and air resistance is negligible, then its speed when it returns to the starting point is the same as when it was released. If air resistance were not negligible, how would its speed upon return compare with its initial speed? How would the maximum height to which it rises be affected?

answer.solution: Air resistance opposes the motion of the object through the air in both directions. On the way up it acts together with gravity, so the object slows more quickly than in free-fall and does not rise as high; on the way down it acts against gravity, so the object gains speed more slowly than in free-fall. The object would therefore return to its starting point with a speed less than the speed at which it was released, and the maximum height it reaches would be less than the height it would reach in free-fall.

exercises.prompt: The severity of a fall depends on your speed when you strike the ground. All factors but the acceleration due to gravity being the same, how many times higher could a safe fall on the Moon be than on Earth (gravitational acceleration on the Moon is about 1/6 that of the Earth)?

answer.solution: For a fall from rest through a height $h$, the speed on striking the ground follows from $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$ with $\kvo = 0$, so that $\kv^2 = 2\kg h$. For the same speed at the ground, the height that can be fallen is $h = \kv^2/2\kg$, which is inversely proportional to the acceleration due to gravity. Since the acceleration due to gravity on the Moon is about one sixth of that on Earth, a safe fall on the Moon could be about six times higher than on Earth.

exercises.prompt: How many times higher could an astronaut jump on the Moon than on Earth if his takeoff speed is the same in both locations (gravitational acceleration on the Moon is about 1/6 of $\kg$ on Earth)?

answer.solution: The astronaut rises until his velocity is zero, and the height reached follows from $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$ with $\kv = 0$, so that the height is $\kvo^2/2\kg$. With the same takeoff speed, the height is inversely proportional to the acceleration due to gravity, and with $\kg$ on the Moon about one sixth of $\kg$ on Earth, the astronaut could jump about six times higher on the Moon.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the displacement and velocity at times of (a) 0.500, (b) 1.00, (c) 1.50, and (d) 2.00 s for a ball thrown straight up with an initial velocity of 15.0 m/s. Take the point of release to be $\kyo = 0$.

parts.hint: Use $\ky = \kyo + \kvo\kt - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$ with $\kt = 0.500$ s, as in Example 2.14.
The ball is almost at its highest point, where the velocity would be zero.
The velocity is now negative: the ball is on its way down, though still above the point of release.

exercises.prompt: A basketball referee tosses the ball straight up for the starting tip-off. At what minimum velocity must a basketball player leave the ground to rise 1.25 m above the floor in an attempt to get the ball?

answer.hint: At the top of the jump the velocity is zero, so $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$ with $\kv = 0$ gives $\kvo$ from the height alone.

exercises.prompt: A dolphin in an aquatic show jumps straight up out of the water at a velocity of 13.0 m/s. (a) List the knowns in this problem. (b) How high does his body rise above the water? To solve this part, first note that the final velocity is now a known and identify its value. Then identify the unknown, and discuss how you chose the appropriate equation to solve for it. After choosing the equation, show your steps in solving for the unknown, checking units, and discuss whether the answer is reasonable. (c) How long is the dolphin in the air? Neglect any effects due to his size or orientation.

parts.hint: The final velocity at the top of the jump is zero, so the velocity-squared equation contains only one unknown, the height.
The dolphin takes as long to fall back to the water as it took to rise, so find the time to the top from $\kv = \kvo - \kg\kt$ and double it.

answer.solution: (a) $\ka = -9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$; $\kvo = 13.0\ \text{m/s}$; $\kyo = 0\ \text{m}$ (b) $\kv = 0\ \text{m/s}$. Unknown is distance $\ky$ to top of trajectory, where velocity is zero. Use equation $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 + 2\ka(\ky - \kyo)$ because it contains all known values except for $\ky$, so we can solve for $\ky$. Solving for $\ky$ gives $$\begin{aligned}\kv^2 - \kvo^2 &= 2\ka(\ky - \kyo)\\ \frac{\kv^2 - \kvo^2}{2\ka} &= \ky - \kyo\\ \ky &= \kyo + \frac{\kv^2 - \kvo^2}{2\ka} = 0\ \text{m} + \frac{(0\ \text{m/s})^2 - (13.0\ \text{m/s})^2}{2(-9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)} = 8.62\ \text{m}\end{aligned}$$ Dolphins measure about 2 meters long and can jump several times their length out of the water, so this is a reasonable result. (c) $2.65\ \text{s}$

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the height of a cliff if it takes 2.35 s for a rock to hit the ground when it is thrown straight up from the cliff with an initial velocity of 8.00 m/s. (b) How long would it take to reach the ground if it is thrown straight down with the same speed?

parts.hint: With up positive, the ground is at $\ky = -h$; put $\kt = 2.35$ s into the position equation and the height is the only unknown.
Thrown down, $\kvo = -8.00$ m/s and $\ky$ is the same; the position equation is now a quadratic in $\kt$, and only the positive root is physical.

exercises.prompt: You throw a ball straight up with an initial velocity of 15.0 m/s. It passes a tree branch on the way up at a height of 7.00 m. How much additional time will pass before the ball passes the tree branch on the way back down?

answer.hint: The position equation with $\ky = 7.00$ m is a quadratic in $\kt$ with two positive roots, one on the way up and one on the way down; the answer is the difference between them.

exercises.prompt: Standing at the base of one of the cliffs of Mt. Arapiles in Victoria, Australia, a hiker hears a rock break loose from a height of 105 m. He can’t see the rock right away but then does, 1.50 s later. (a) How far above the hiker is the rock when he can see it? (b) How much time does he have to move before the rock hits his head?

parts.hint: The rock falls from rest, so in 1.50 s it drops $\tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$ from the 105 m.
Find the whole time of the fall through 105 m and subtract the 1.50 s that has already passed.

exercises.prompt: There is a 250-m-high cliff at Half Dome in Yosemite National Park in California. Suppose a boulder breaks loose from the top of this cliff. (a) How fast will it be going when it strikes the ground? (b) Assuming a reaction time of 0.300 s, how long will a tourist at the bottom have to get out of the way after hearing the sound of the rock breaking loose (neglecting the height of the tourist, which would become negligible anyway if hit)? The speed of sound is 335 m/s on this day.

parts.hint: The boulder falls from rest through 250 m; $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$ gives its speed, and the velocity is downward, so it is negative.
The sound takes 250 m at 335 m/s to reach the tourist; take that time and the reaction time away from the time of the fall.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you drop a rock into a dark well and, using precision equipment, you measure the time for the sound of a splash to return. (a) Neglecting the time required for sound to travel up the well, calculate the distance to the water if the sound returns in 2.0000 s. (b) Now calculate the distance taking into account the time for sound to travel up the well. The speed of sound is 332.00 m/s in this well.

parts.hint: If the whole 2.0000 s is the time of the fall, the depth is $\tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$.
The 2.0000 s is the time of the fall plus the time the sound takes to climb the depth $d$ at 332.00 m/s; write both in terms of $d$ and solve the quadratic.

exercises.prompt: A coin is dropped from a hot-air balloon that is 300 m above the ground and rising at 10.0 m/s upward. For the coin, find (a) the maximum height reached, (b) its position and velocity 4.00 s after being released, and (c) the time before it hits the ground.

parts.hint: The coin leaves the balloon moving up at 10.0 m/s, so it rises until its velocity is zero before it falls; measure heights from the ground.
Put $\kt = 4.00$ s into the position equation with $\kyo = 300$ m and $\kvo = 10.0$ m/s.
Use $\kv = \kvo - \kg\kt$; the coin is falling by then, so its velocity is negative.
Set $\ky = 0$ in the position equation and keep the positive root of the quadratic.
